## Changed

- `model`: the stone piers are the parts of the ground-floor walls outside the
  envelope, cut at it, instead of whole wall pieces lying mostly outside it. A
  pier that runs on into the house is stone outside and a wall inside, and a part
  nowhere thicker than 10 cm — a wall drawn a few centimetres past the envelope —
  is no longer a pier. On the reference dossier `stone_piers` goes from 7 to 2
  and the ground floor gains the partition the pier continues into; on the
  corpus, dossier 9 loses its 10 pieces (column corners straddling a derived
  envelope) and dossier 13 one 4 cm strip. `golden.rs` applies the rule to the
  prototype's ground floor before comparing.
- `model`: the parapet is the one the roof plan draws — its white bands 7 to
  15 cm thick lying on the roof, joined into a ring and cut to the outline —
  instead of a `parapet_width_m` ring along the roof's edge. On the reference
  dossier it now stands 37 cm in from the curved edges, where the roof plan and
  the section draw it (6.54 → 4.64 m²). A roof plan that draws no such ring keeps
  the edge ring and says so in `warnings`, as dossiers 3, 9, 11, 12, 13 and 14
  do. `golden.rs` no longer compares the parapet's area with the prototype's; it
  checks that the parapet is one ring on the roof.
- `model`: the stone piers' heights come off the elevations. Each elevation's
  level marks and grid bubbles place it against the model; each pier is
  projected onto it, and the filled face as wide as the pier there — the nearest
  pier's, where two project onto one — gives its top. `model.stone[]` carries
  `top` and `top_pages` when the elevations agree within 5 cm, the glTF and the
  GeoJSON extrude the pier to it rather than to the parapet, and `params` lists
  the sheets in `elevation_pages`. On the reference dossier both stone walls stop
  at +4.800, where all four facades draw them, instead of rising through the
  roof. A pier fewer than two elevations draw, or whose elevations disagree,
  keeps the parapet height with a `warnings` entry — one sheet alone may be a
  section filed as an elevation (dossier 13's page 40 is).
- `model`: a slab's edge band comes off the section and the plans. Where a
  section cuts a slab, the outermost fill at the slab's height at either end is
  read as a profile — how far the band reaches past the slab, how tall its tip
  stands, which face slopes and over what run — and kept when both ends agree.
  The plans place it: the band runs along the slab's edges that strips as wide
  as it lie beside, on the storey's own plan or else the roof plan.
  `model.floors[].edge` and `model.roof.edge` carry the profile and the runs
  (`inner` along the slab, `outer` along the tip, vertex facing vertex), the
  glTF and the GeoJSON extrude the band in three steps, `params` lists the
  sheets in `section_pages`, and the roof's outline gives up the band the roof
  plan's strips had joined to it. On the reference dossier both slabs end in a
  band 0.40 m past the slab down both ends and round the front — the storey's
  rising to +3.70 with its top sloping, the roof's to +7.30 sloping underneath —
  the roof's area goes from 100.87 to 94.39 m² and its parapet, cut to it, from
  4.64 to 4.17 m². The sketch set changes alike and no other dossier of the
  corpus does. A band a section cuts that no plan draws leaves the slab square,
  with a `warnings` entry.
- `model`: the materials come off the callouts. The elevations, the sections
  and the roof plan label what each surface is made of; each callout — the
  runs on one baseline, split where a wide gap separates two — is read against
  tables of word stems for the part it names (walls, glazing, railings, stone
  piers, roof, parapet, slabs, plinth) and the material (travertine, basalt,
  felsite, tuff, rough stone, stone, plaster, concrete, metal, metal sheet,
  glass), spelt as the drafter spelt it (`ՏՐԱՎԵՏՐԻՆԵ`, `ՄԵՏՂԱԿԱՆ`, `ՔԱՆԵ`).
  `model.materials` gives each part the material the most sheets name, with the
  first callout's text and the pages; a part named in two materials keeps the
  commoner and says so in `warnings`. The glTF and the GeoJSON colour each
  element by its part's material, the ground storey's slab as the plinth. On
  the reference dossier eight parts read — travertine walls, rough stone piers,
  a stone parapet, metal railings, glass, a metal-sheet roof, concrete slabs, a
  basalt plinth — and the back facade's plaster walls are the warning. Across
  the corpus, dossier 3 reads plaster walls, dossier 9 a metal-sheet roof over
  concrete slabs, and dossier 10 a metal-sheet roof and stone walls, whose
  callouts name plaster on the same sheets (a warning); the other dossiers call
  nothing out the tables know.
